item.title: At Present: art, books, and thinking about digital creativity
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
What I’ve been…

Working on

The main thing I’ve been working on this week is my website: nicolebergenart.com

It’s a creative meandering experience and you’re welcome to stop by anytime.

I created it as a place to share my work and any facet of myself that I want without having the needs of “the algorithm” in the back of my mind! A place to be more free on the internet than Instagram allows and just be a weird, whole human. 

Zuzu/Eli Trier talked about "idiosyncrasy as resistance" in her last video, and I thought, “hey, I can do that!”

And also, gouache portraits & figures with Draw Brighton, as usual. This is the model Mariana and she's incredible.

And some intuitive plant painting inspired by Orla Stevens' Patreon workshops lately:

Bindweed/The Devil - the possible beginnings of a far-off future tarot deck?

Reading

The Fauves by Nathalia Brodskaia. I got it from the library and loved it so much I found a used copy on eBay!

Elaine de Kooning: Portraits by Brandon Brame Fortune. Also found on eBay. I love art books so much but they’re so expensive (thank god for libraries). 

Listening to

I binged the entirety of botanical studies of internet magic by Kening Zhu in about three days. Then I listened to it all again!

She's also absolutely brilliant at naming things. Just check out the list of her episode titles!

Thinking About

Analogue media and digital creativity. I want a way to be my whole creative self  online without having to consider a tech bro at any point in the process. More on analogue media later!

Inspired by

Zuzu's Haus of Cats (I borrowed the idea for this newsletter format from her, so you should definitely check her out):

Kening Zhu's entirely online world.

Samira Addi/Mimma:

She's been my portrait inspiration lately. How gorgeous is this?!

item.title: Nature journaling done “wrong”
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
Went to the Calgary Nature Journal Club at the Twelve Mile Coolee today and saw water hemlock for the first time so I had to draw that!

I didn’t do the nature journaling “properly”, but who cares. I was out in a beautiful ravine drawing and painting with other people. It was a delight.

If you do want to know what “properly” looks like, John Muir Law does some very cool things around nature, education, and art.

wp:comment.wp:comment_content: The beauty of nature journaling is there isn’t a wrong way to do it. I loved your little painting. I admire your focus on capturing the colour and feel of the space. There are specific prompts you can do and some are more scientific note taking but some can also just be capturing a moment. I was sad I didn’t get the time to look through your little book because I was going to get to yours next in the gallery walk and everyone started to pack up.
Usually, I’m out drawing by myself, so it was lovely to meet everyone and have a group to draw outside with. I love that everyone did things it their own way. 💜

item.title: Pigments of many colours
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
I’m such a geek. I’ve made a spreadsheet of all the pigments I either use or want to try and the gouache and acrylic paints that are available at my local shops that are made with these pigments.

I’ve also made individual swatches of each colour in my various non-paint art supply kits. For instance, I have three plein air options, plus a couple for portraits and one for miscellaneous.

And then I put them on little clasp rings.

It’s just so much fun to be able to play with colour combinations without having to start a new page for each combination.

I didn’t swatch my acrylic colours because there would be entirely too many combinations, but I did swatch my gouache colours.

(Ignore the dusty keyboard!)

That being said, I have played with other ways of colour mixing and swatching my acrylic paints.

It’s always so satisfying to see what colours you can get just through mixing a few pigments.

item.title: Tansy/Strength (new tarot painting)
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
The tansy flower essence that I got from The Poison Garden’s apothecary is helpful for neurodivergent people, in particular, to calm overwhelming emotions. The creator describes it as “emotional protection for sensitive souls”. 

Tansy is also a highly effective (and dangerous) abortifacient, so I’ve always associated it with women’s (or anyone with a uterus’) sovereignty over our own bodies. In the wake of Dolly Parton’s death, it seems like a good fit for me now that I’m trying to be unapologetically myself in this funny little online world, perhaps with too few rhinestones. 

In the photography deck I’ve made, I’ve matched it up with the Strength card for its tenacity and connection (for me) to women’s power.

item.title: Books Lately: data feminism, AI, and activism
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
Data Feminism by Catherine D'Ignazio, Lauren F. Klein

This was such a helpful book for me, as a data analyst. I’m always trying to be more aware of when data is missing or skewed in ways that the “universal” (white male) viewer might not notice. I was constantly looking things up and now I have a bunch of tabs open with all the things I’m thinking about or hoping to work on. 

The Worlds I See by Dr. Fei-Fei Li

I enjoy any scientist’s enthusiasm and wonder around their subject and I’m glad she got into the ethics of AI, but I think it’s a bit unfortunate that that only happened in the last little section of the book. I think scientists have a social responsibility to imagine the uses of their creations by the tech billionaires because those billionaires have no sense of ethics or responsibility to anyone other than themselves and their shareholders and most politicians are no better. I know it’s hard because the technology is so cool in itself, but it’s also harming both people and the environment. 

No!: The Art and Activism of Complaining by Sara Ahmed

One of those books that contains all sorts of useful information that the people who most need to read and absorb will probably ignore. Now I’ll always think of “Complaints [as] missing data”. Main takeaways: work with other people as much as possible and document everything!

item.title: Books lately (non-fiction edition)
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
We Do This 'Til We Free Us by Mariame Kaba

An incredible thought-provoking book full of all manner of challenging and interesting ideas. I’ll have to mull these over for a while and, probably, reread it some time. I’m not 100% convinced that the legal system can never provide justice (I guess that depends how you define justice), but it sure doesn’t seem to do that for women, trans people, or people of colour very often, so we definitely need better ideas.

(I’m in Canada but on the prairies our police originated to remove Indigenous people from their homes to make room for white settlers, so the situation is different than the American one but not better. Except for the for-profit prison thing. There currently aren’t any in Canada and there are many problems with Canadian prisons but making prisons for-profit seems like a magnet for unethical behavior and not on the part of the prisoners. And the death penalty.) 

Separation of Church and Hate by John Fugelsang

I tend to prefer books like The Bible Says So by Dan McClellen but I’m not entirely sure I’m the target audience for this one as a leftist Canadian! I did grow up with people who chose a religion of hate and I’m not convinced that all these arguments will convince them, but maybe some are worth a try. For instance, the idea that the extremists would be against gay marriage but not straight divorce is inaccurate,l; in my experience, the extremists I know are against both. Basically, I’m not entirely sure what to make of this book but I hope it can help some people. 

A Truce That Is Not Peace by Miriam Toews

I know the format of this memoir isn’t for everyone but I loved it. It seems familiar, a bit like stream of consciousness with all the stops, starts, and detours. My only complaint is that it’s too short!

The Secret Lives of Colour by Kassia St Clair

Such a fascinating, geeky book. I loved learning where and how pigments originated alongside some past associations with an incredible range of colours from around the world. 

The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After Al by Cory Doctorow

I appreciate that in both this and Enshittification, he lays out clear (though not easy) things that ordinary people can do to stand up to the rich who are trying to control everything. His books somehow manage to be both infuriating and encouraging simultaneously.

item.title: Making poppets & war water
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
I collected some yarrow and smooth broom grass, some cherry, rowan, and elder twigs to make some poppets. I haven’t finished them or put them to use yet because they’re still drying out, but I’m glad I have them.

I’ll probably add some fabric in certain colours and a few other ingredients as needed.

I also made some war water.

I don’t have a specific use case right now but I’m beginning to think I should have something handy in case someone needs to see some consequences or be encouraged to keep their distance.

Combine stagnant storm water, white wine far, rusted nails, cayenne, nettle, wormwood, vinegar, hawthorn thorns, burdock burrs, cemetery dirt, ash, blue pigment. Shake. Start on Tuesday for war and finish on Wednesday for wisdom.

Incantation went adding the nails:

  • For nail of one, you’d better run 
  • For nail of two, I’m coming for you
  • For nail of three, you will never be free
  • For nail of four, you are no more. 

Incantation when finished mixing: Causing darkness and consequences, I release maleficent energies.

This recipe is adapted from Underneath the Veil of Marigold’s on YouTube.

item.title: Reading Lately
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
Gothic lit, reading around the world, and other adventure

Practical Magic 2: The Book of Magic by Alice Hoffman

Such good fun, right from the start. I love these books. They always make me feel witchier and more adventurous. 

Final Orbit by Chris Hadfield

I’m a sucker for anything NASA and this was good fun. I breezed through it and, while it didn’t always keep me guessing, it was always entertaining. 

The Hacienda by Isabel Cañas (Mexico)

Creepy and ferocious. I took a while to warm up to the main character but I related to her confusion – there were many times I didn’t know what was about to happen next! Just as good as Vampires of El Norte, it also takes gothic genre conventions and distorts them just a little so that it’s incredibly satisfying. I love a good haunted gothic manor. 

The Bewitching by Silvia Moreno-Garcia (Mexico/Canada)

I do love a witchy story. This was compelling, though by the third quarter I began to feel it was getting a tiny bit repetitive and could have been wrapped up a little sooner. 

The Night Circus and other stories by Uršul’a Kovalyk (Slovakia)

There wasn’t a story I thought wasn’t powerful in some way and all were delightfully strange. I need to find more of her writing. All of her characters were the most bizarre people, so full-of-life and none of them fit neatly into the society they lived in. 

Pure Colour by Shelia Heti

An oddly beautiful philosophical story told in tiny moments and full of wonder. It has very little plot but focuses on how we define our relationships, how we can know other people or ourselves, and how we love people. It’s about loss and death but in the most radiant way. It hypothesises about second chances, second lives, and second worlds: cosmic do-overs. And sometimes, second deaths. It was also sometimes funny, not in a laugh-out-loud sort of way but in a smiling through the tears sort of way. 

Near to the Wild Heart by Clarice Lispector (Brazil)

Holy Virginia Woolf. Why have I not read more Lispector? Joana is a force of nature, such a vibrant character who is compelling if not exactly likeable. Even so, she is, somehow, relatable. Perhaps I shouldn’t admit to that!

Death Takes Me by Cristina Rivera Garza (Mexico)

Wow, that was weird! I knew it was a mystery but wasn’t sure what to expect. It turns out, it’s impossible to know what to expect! I was surprised by the weirdness at the beginning, but it got my attention. It’s anything but a normal detective story, all short sentences from two characters obsessed with poetry and ideas around expectation, gender and violence. I’m not sure I liked it but I did keep listening. 

I think it’s more allegory than crime novel but allegory for what I’m not sure. With the excessive number of penises, I think it’s trying to make a point about gendered violence and how female victims are treated by society, but I’m not sure what that point is. And something to do with Argentinian poet Alejandra Pizarnik that I didn’t understand at all until the essay that appeared halfway through the book.

I don’t know if it’s the translation but the excessive use of sentence fragments, and sometimes just a bunch of single words hanging in the air, became quite grating. If she was going for the brevity and “crystalline prose” that Pizarnik admired, I’m not sure this is it. Ideas in sentence fragments might work in a 10-20 line prose poem, but in a novel, it doesn’t have at all the same effect and feels a bit like the novel went through the blender. 

The second half was much better than the first, or maybe I just got used to it, I’m not sure. But I still have no idea which I just read!

item.title: Reading lately
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
Non-fiction: witchcraft, history, and memoir

Sigil Witchery by Laura Tempest Zakroff

Good fun and easy to get into. It’s a fun way to play with sigils and I think it’s probably accessible to non-artists. I will be doodling with more intentionality sometimes now. In addition to how to make them, it also includes quite a lot of creative ways to use them. I like that she encourages people to put aside the childhood bagage about not being able to draw and just try. It really does just take practice. 

Saturday is for Funerals by Unity Dow & Max Essex (Botswana)

A valuable collection of reminiscences from Botswana shortly after the height of the AIDS crisis when ARVs were widely available but the stigma was still hard to overcome. The memories from Unity Dow are a good way to put faces on complicated and emotional problems and they’re supplemented by political and scientific commentary by Max Essex that can provide context and help you understand people’s situations and decisions. 

Finding my Way by Malala Yousafzai

It was good to read her perspective of growing up and becoming an adult separate from all the media and social media circuses. Sometimes I think too many people expect too much from one person, and not just about Malala, as though one person can solve all the world’s problems while absolving others from responsibility. That said, I do love her work around girls' education and I’m heartbroken and horrified for the Afghan girls who can’t go to school or live free in any way anymore. And I’m glad she’s gotten to go back to Pakistan sometimes despite all the death threats.

item.title: Books Lately
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
The Green Crow by Kristīne Ulberga (Latvia)

I immediately loved the main character and her possibly hallucinated crow. It also highlighted one of my many issues with mental health professionals—it’s hard to get help when you need it but after you’ve been diagnosed, everything can be associated with a symptom, even normal activities and feelings. I know that it’s hard to separate normal unpleasant feelings from the more harmful ones (having some experience in this area) but not everything needs to be pathologised. And in the case of this woman, she may have a psychological problem that predates her abusive husband, but he seems to be her main problem. If the psychiatric hospital is doing anything helpful for her, it seems to be mostly in giving her a reprieve from him. This story has also brought forward the ways in which men have used psychiatric problems, real or imagined, to manipulate and control women. It’s quite surrealist in places and a bit too plausible in others. 

The Thursday Murder Club by Richard Osman

I needed to read something more lighthearted after a couple other recent reads and, today, that was an irreverent murder mystery. It turned out to be delightful with more than a hint of Miss Marple, which I’ll never complain about. I loved this cast of characters and I’ll have to read the next one!

The Seed Keeper by Diane Wilson (Sicangu Oyate (Lakota))

Rosalie’s story is so moving. We really do need to find a way to live with the land in a healthier way but it’s hard to imagine ways to do that when you’re up against governments and multinational corporations. I suppose everyone just has to do what they can to live in a better way. Seeds really are tiny miracles and the soil and water give us life. There’s so much suffering in the world but we really don’t need to do this to each other.  This was an extraordinary book and the blurb just can’t do it justice. 

The Savage Detectives by Roberto Bolaño (Chile)

My first thought on reading this book was that it was most definitely written by a man. The first and third sections felt completely different from the largest second section which went on too long and took itself too seriously. I would have enjoyed it more if there were fewer characters to keep track of. The little glimpses into people’s lives were interesting and I liked parts of it but I didn’t love this book the way other people do. 

The Name of the Rose by Umberto Eco (Italy)

I tried reading this about a year or so ago and couldn’t get into it but I really enjoyed it this time. I think, with the slow pace and avalanche of theological debates, I had to be in the right mood for it. It was a fun, twisty mystery that seems like it might have inspired Dan Brown’s Inferno, but it’s much more intellectual and much less pop culture. 

The Wind That Lays Waste By Selva Almada (Argentina)

This was a sharp little novella. It’s always frustrating to me to listen to preaching, even in fiction, but that’s religious trauma for you. I wanted that character to be more respectful to the others but he couldn’t see past his worldview, which often happens. It was a sparse and beautifully translated short book. 

The Secret Place by Tana French (Ireland)

This was a fun mystery, although the way the teenage girls spoke and treated each other, while not inaccurate, was annoying. But I guess that can just be an annoying stage of life. It certainly didn’t make me nostalgic for junior high or high school, but nothing can do that! Overall, it was a fun mystery and a pretty good exploration of the precariousness of important friendships when big transitions happen.

I haven't read The Last Mandarin yet, but that's a sneak peek of what I'm reading next!

item.title: About
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
The inspiration for this site

I’ve become deeply unsatisfied with social media and I’ve been looking for alternatives but they’re mostly variations on the same themes. I want something freer. Somewhere I can feel at home.

My inspirations for this weird little corner of the internet are Eli Trier/Zuzu from the incredible Haus of Cats and Kening Zhu from the perfectly named botanical studies of internet magic. (She really is brilliant at naming things - have a look at the list of podcast episodes!) So I'm off on a little adventure to see what I can make online that might not be what anyone expects, and certainly isn't what anyone suggests, but that is completely mine.

Lately, I’ve been thinking of this site as an old manor house in a gothic novel with winding staircases, secret rooms. So far, this involves a hidden room in the library and a mysterious ghost.

The thing that finally set me in motion on this journey was this video, and to that end, let's make the internet weird again, indeed.

The Madwoman

I'm a weirdo from the Canadian prairies who is interested in almost everything except for the grind of modern life. I have no interest in the corporate ladder and would rather be a quirky hobbit making art and reading books in a little apartment with a balcony garden. When I have the energy, I'll bake muffins.

My artistic journey

I've always had creative projects on the go, from collage to crochet, but last year a local art shop had a going out of business sale and I decided to buy some paints. Not because I knew how to paint, but it seemed like fun. Call it a mid-life crisis!

I began to learn via Art Prof and quite a lot of making a good mess. I've been inspired by many artists on YouTube (someday I'll collate this into a blog post!) and have joined the Patreons of Orla Stevens of The Outdoor Sketchbook Collective and children's book illustrator Emma Carlisle where I can study and practice with both experienced, trained artists, and self-taught artists like myself.

Regarding landscapes

I always thought I couldn't paint representationally, so I began by exploring mixed media and texture while trying to find something essential in my local prairie landscape. I’ve been playing with approaches to abstraction, atmosphere, and tone in my work lately. 

Regarding portraits & figures

And then I decided to do something bonkers and tried to draw a person. The first ones were a bit wobbly, but, as with most things, I found it just takes practice and persistance. I've since joined Draw Brighton's Patreon for access to models (I love the respect with which they treat all their models) and am having so much fun.

item.title: Dipping my toes into still life
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
Here’s me dipping my toes into still life with Emma Carlisle’s slow still life session. Her Patreon is so varied with vastly different subject matter every month and it always stretches me out nicely.

I’m not very experienced or comfortable with still life. Composition isn’t my strong suit! But all the more reason to practice.

I’m not particularly interested in realism but I enjoyed the contrast between more precise parts and the looser ones. And I think I’ve improved quite a bit since my first couple attempts at still life.

We do owe each other something. Caring for people is a prerequisite for living in my little world.

I'm not sure exactly what this page will look like, but one of the things I do on Instagram is keep an eye on the work of human rights and environmental justice organisations, among others. I do want people to know where I stand on certain issues and I need to find ways to keep updated about things I care about without social media (newsletters!).

For instance, I've been calling the atrocities in Gaza ethnic cleansing since well before October 7, 2023 and a genocide since I read Amnesty International's report "Israel/Occupied Palestinian Territory: ‘You Feel Like You Are Subhuman’: Israel’s Genocide Against Palestinians in Gaza".

I'll add to this page eventually, but in the meantime, suffice to say, I'm a fan of:

  • human rights (including trans rights and Indigenous rights)
  • environmental protection (including water rights and protection and Indigenous stewardship and sovereignty)
  • some sort of overhaul of the legal (I can't call it justice) system
  • black lives mattering to everyone
  • most struggles that I'm aware of against the multinational corporations that are trying to control everything from seed saving to surveillance
  • civil rights and liberties, including online

and all manner of grassroots, community-centred, and Indigenous-led initiatives. I'm probably forgetting many things right now, but I'll add to this non-exhaustive list later.

item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
You found the secret room in the library! Let me know your favourite fandom or geeky obsession here:

The Doctor's Library: all the books in Doctor Who, from the 9th-12th doctors

I compiled this list in 2018, so forgive me but I can no longer remember if I have all the right citations. It took about a year to collect all this and I apologise for the questionable formatting.

At a certain point, I stopped writing things up and just trailed off with bullet-point notes.

I always meant to organise this into a bookshelf of some sort.

The 9th Doctor: Christopher Eccleston

S1, E3 The Unquiet Dead: Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol, The Old Curiosity Shop, The Mystery of Edwin Drood,

The only Dickens’ novel I have ever read is A Christmas Carol, but I know that the lives and difficulties of orphans come up repeatedly in Dickens’ work. In Bleak House, Oliver Twist, The Old Curiosity Shop, and Great Expectations, Esther Summerson, Oliver Twist, Nell Trent, and Pip are all orphans. In “The Unquiet Dead”, Gwynth is an orphan working for a mortuary, which seems a suitable setting for a Dickens episode given his preoccupations with crime and poverty.  

On arrival, the Doctor says they’re in Naples on December 24, 1860 in Naples. In early 1845, as part of a larger European tour, Dickens did go to Naples. He returned in 1853 and published a short story “The Italian Prisoner”, which was set in that area.

http://www.victorianweb.org/authors/dickens/gallery/tours.html Great Expectations began publication as a serial in December 1860. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Expectations

In the first scene in which Dickens appears there is a poster behind him for a reading in Cardiff on December 24, 1969. The real Dickens did do readings between 1968-1970 but not in December of 1969 due to health problems

Ghosts appear in A Christmas Carol and ghost-like figures appear in “The Unquiet Dead” as the Gelth and the bodies they take over.

 “I’m like a ghost, condemned to repeat myself though all of eternity”—Charles Dickens in “The Unquiet Dead”.

The first time Rose and the Doctor see Dickens, he’s in a theatre reciting an abridged part of stave one of A Christmas Carol, and is interrupted just before talk of ghosts by the dead woman glowing and then emitting what seems to be a ghost.

“Now, it is a fact that there was nothing at all particular about the knocker on the door, except that it was very large. It is also a fact that Scrooge had seen it, night and morning, during his whole residence in that place; also that Scrooge had as little of what is called fancy about him as any man in the City of London, even including--which is a bold word--the corporation, aldermen, and livery. Let it also be borne in mind. that Scrooge had not bestowed one thought on Marley since his last mention of his seven-years'-dead partner that afternoon. And then let any man explain to me, if he can, how it happened that Scrooge, having his key in the lock of the door, saw in the knocker, without its undergoing any intermediate process of change--not a knocker, but Marley's face. Marley's face. It was not in impenetrable shadow, as the other objects in the yard were, but had a dismal light about it, like a bad lobster in a dark cellar. It was not angry or ferocious, but looked at Scrooge as Marley used to look: with ghostly spectacles turned up on its ghostly forehead.”—Charles Dickens, A Christmas Carol

When the Doctor gets into Dickens’ coach, he exclaims “You’re brilliant, you are!” and says he’s read all of his work and calls him a genius after which Dickens agrees that he can stay in the coach. The doctor says he’s the number one fan of Dickens before criticizing the “American bit” of Martin Chuzzlewit. He then says “Do the death of Little Nell. It cracks me up”. Oscar Wilde once said “You would need to have a heart of stone not to laugh at the death of little Nell.” (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens#cite_note-149)

When the doctor interrupts this discussion to tell the driver to go faster so they can get Rose back, Dickens asks why he was “wasting my time talking about dry old books. This is much more important”.

Charles Dickens & the Doctor in “The Unquiet Dead”.

When Dickens and the Doctor arrive at the mortuary, Dickens says “What the Shakespeare is going on?”

Sidebar: “Mistress Page. I cannot tell what the dickens his name is my
husband had him of. What do you call your knight's
name, sirrah?” –Shakespeare, The Merry Wives of Windsor, Act 3, Scene 2

Merriam-Webster defines “dickens” as “devil” https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/dickens

On entering the morgue: “Talk about Bleak House” –The doctor

Near the end, Dickens quotes Shakespeare, saying “There are more things in heaven and earth, [Horatio], Than are dreamt of in your philosophy” --Hamlet, Act 1, Scene 5

At the end, Dickens decides to use his experiences of the Gelth for the ending of The Mystery of Edwin Drood, “Perhaps the killer was not the boy’s uncle. Perhaps he was not of this earth!...The Mystery of Edwin Drood and the Blue Elementals”. He died before finishing, as the doctor knew he would. When Dickens asked if his books last the Doctor responds that they last forever.

The episode ends with Dickens walking down the street, saying “God bless us, every one!” which Tiny Tim says at the Christmas dinner in A Christmas Carol, a phrase Dickens repeats at the end of the novella.

P.S.

This is the first episode that Mark Gatiss wrote for Doctor Who. He subsequently wrote wrote "The Idiot's Lantern” (S2, E7), "Victory of the Daleks" (S5, E3), "Night Terrors" (S6, E9), "Cold War" (S7, E8), "The Crimson Horror" (S7, E11), "Robot of Sherwood" (S8, E3), "Sleep No More" (S9, E9), and "Empress of Mars" (S10, E9). He has written four Doctor Who novels Nightshade, St Anthony's Fire, The Roundheads, and Last of the Gaderene. He has acted in three Doctor Who episodes: "The Lazarus Experiment" in (S3, E6), "The Wedding of River Song" (S6, E13), and "Twice Upon a Time" (2017 Christmas Special after series 13). He has written three Lucifer Box spy novels: The Vesuvius Club, The Devil in Amber, Black Butterfly.

S1, E9 The Empty Child: Star Trek

Ok, so I’m just using the fact that there have been Star Trek books published to include this. When they land in London at the beginning of this episode, Rose said “Not very “Spock”, is it” referring to the Doctor just asking people if they’d noticed an unusual bang in the middle of London rather than doing “a scan for alien tech”. “I think you should do a scan for alien tech. Give me some Spock, for once. Would it kill you?”

When Jack Harkness did exactly this a little while later she said “very Spock” and she told him her “time agent” companion was “Mr. Spock” aka the Doctor.

The Doctor: “Mr. Spock?”

Rose: “What was I supposed to say? You don’t have a name. Don’t you ever get tired of Doctor? Doctor who?”

The Doctor: “Nine centuries in. I’m coping”.

The Doctor: “Feeding frenzy for the homeless kids of London town. Puddings for all, as long as the bombs don’t get you…

Nancy: “Something wrong with that?

The Doctor: Wrong? It’s brilliant! I’m not sure if it’s Marxism in action or a West End musical.

The 10th Doctor: David Tennant

Christmas Special 2005 The Christmas Invasion: The Lion King, The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy

The Lion King “From the day they arrive on the planet and, blinking, step into the sun, there is more to see than can ever be seen, more to do than…”

After beating the Sycorax in a duel, he says “Not bad for a man in his jim jams. Very Arthur Dent. Now, there was a nice man”, a reference to The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy in which Arthur Dent spends several years wandering around space in his bathrobe. Hitchhiker’s author Douglas Adams wrote for Doctor Who during the tenure of the 4th doctor.

Rose helping the doctor into a bathrobe.

S2, E2 Tooth & Claw: “Books are the best weapons in the world”, Torchwood Library, Queen Victoria

“Since my husband’s death, I find myself with more of a taste for supernatural fiction…And that’ the charm of a ghost story, isn’t it? Not the scares and chills, that’s just for children, but the hope of some contact from the great beyond.” –Queen Victoria

After which Sir Robert tells a story of a wolf and a missing child once per generation.

 “You want weapons? We’re in a library. Books! Best weapons in the world. This room’s the greatest arsenal we could have. Arm yourself!” –The Doctor

The Doctor, Rose, Queen Victoria, & Sir Robert in the Torchwood Library

S2, E5 The Girl in the Fireplace: My Fair Lady

After dancing with Madame de Pompadour, the doctor returns to the broken spaceship singing, somewhat drunkenly, “I could have danced all night, I could have danced all night, and still have begged for more. I could have spread my wings and done a th—“ from My Fair Lady, which is based on the play Pygmalion by Bernard Shaw.

S3, E1 Smith and Jones: Emily Pankhurst

Martha asks the Doctor if he has a laser spanner. He says he did, but it was stolen by Emily (Emmeline) Pankhurst, “cheeky woman”, a British activist for women’s rights and educational and social reforms who published her autobiography, My Own Story, in 1914. In it, she describes her experiences of being able to read from a very young age.

S3, E2 The Shakespeare Code: Love’s Labour’s Lost, Sonnet 18, “57 academics just punched the air” regarding his possible bisexuality. expelliarmus “Good old J.K.?” , cites Dylan Thomas’s poem “Do not go gentle into that good night” “Rage, rage against the dying of the light”

-J.K. Rowling & the doctor got read HP before release & has a “collection of all 11 Harry Potter books” on the TARDIS.

-Elizabeth I (The Tudors)

Set in London 1599

DOCTOR: Oh, yes, the Globe Theatre! Brand new. Just opened. Through, strictly speaking, it's not a globe, it's a tetradecagon. Fourteen sides. Containing the man himself.
MARTHA: Whoa, you don't mean. Is Shakespeare in there?
DOCTOR: Oh, yes. Miss Jones, will you accompany me to the theatre?

MARTHA: That's amazing! Just amazing. It's worth putting up with the smell. And those are men dressed as women, yeah?
DOCTOR: London never changes.
MARTHA: Where's Shakespeare? I want to see Shakespeare. Author! Author! Do people shout that? Do they shout Author?
MAN: Author! Author!
(And the crowd take up the chant.)
DOCTOR: Well, they do now.
(Shakespeare comes onto the stage, very full of himself, to rapturous applause.)
MARTHA: He's a bit different from his portraits.
(Lilith is dressed like an aristocrat, and sitting alone in one of the upper boxes. She takes a rough doll with a strand of hair stuck to its head from her purse.)
DOCTOR: Genius. He's a genius. The genius. The most human human there's ever been. Now we're going to hear him speak. Always he chooses the best words. New, beautiful, brilliant words.
SHAKESPEARE: Ah, shut your big fat mouths!
(Laughter.)
DOCTOR: Oh, well.
MARTHA: You should never meet your heroes.
SHAKESPEARE: You've got excellent taste, I'll give you that. Oh, that's a wig.
(Lilith pulls the hair on her doll.)
LILITH: Wind the craft of ancient harm. The time approaches for our charm.
SHAKESPEARE: I know what you're all saying. Loves Labour's Lost, that's a funny ending, isn't it? It just stops. Will the boys get the girls? Well, don't get your hose in a tangle, you'll find out soon. Yeah, yeah. All in good time. You don't rush a genius.
(Lilith kisses her doll and Shakespeare suddenly goes rigid and blank.)
SHAKESPEARE: When? Tomorrow night. The premiere of my brand new play. A sequel, no less, and I call it Loves Labour's Won.
(A short while later, everyone is filing out of the theatre.)
MARTHA: I'm not an expert, but I've never heard of Loves Labour's Won.
DOCTOR: Exactly. The lost play. It doesn't exist, only in rumours. It's mentioned in lists of his plays but never ever turns up. And no one knows why.

SHAKESPEARE: And you, Sir Doctor. How can a man so young have eyes so old?
DOCTOR: I do a lot of reading.
SHAKESPEARE: A trite reply. Yeah, that's what I'd do.

MARTHA: So, magic and stuff. That's a surprise. It's all a little bit Harry Potter.
DOCTOR: Wait till you read book seven. (published 2007) Oh, I cried.

DOCTOR: The columns there, right? Fourteen sides. I've always wondered, but I never asked. Tell me, Will. Why fourteen sides?
SHAKESPEARE: It was the shape Peter Streete thought best, that's all. Said it carried the sound well.
DOCTOR: Fourteen. Why does that ring a bell? Fourteen.
MARTHA: There's fourteen lines in a sonnet.
DOCTOR: So there is. Good point. Words and shapes following the same design. Fourteen lines, fourteen sides, fourteen facets. Oh, my head. Tetradecagon. Think, think, think! Words, letters, numbers, lines!
SHAKESPEARE: This is just a theatre.
DOCTOR: Oh yeah, but a theatre's magic, isn't it? You should know. Stand on this stage, say the right words with the right emphasis a the right time. Oh, you can make men weep, or cry with joy. Change them. You can change people's minds just with words in this place.

[Southwark]

SHAKESPEARE: So, tell me of Freedonia, where women can be doctors, writers, actors.
MARTHA: This country's ruled by a woman.
SHAKESPEARE: Ah, she's royal. That's God's business. Though you are a royal beauty.
MARTHA: Whoa, Nelly. I know for a fact you've got a wife in the country.
SHAKESPEARE: But Martha, this is Town.
DOCTOR: Come on. We can all have a good flirt later.
SHAKESPEARE: Is that a promise, Doctor?
DOCTOR: Oh, fifty seven academics just punched the air. Now move!

[Globe stage]

BURBAGE: Loves Labour's Won. I don't think much of sequels. They're never as good as the original.
KEMPE: Have you seen this last bit? He must have been dozing off when he wrote that. I don't even know what it means.
BURBAGE: Yeah? Well, that goes for most of his stuff. Ah, but at least it's my speech. Ah ha! I get centre stage. (reads) The light of Shadmock's hollow moon doth shine onto a point in space betwixt Dravidian shores
(A wind suddenly blows through the auditorium.)
KEMPE: What was that?
BURBAGE: Dravidian shores linear five nine three oh one six

SHAKESPEARE: I've been mad. I've lost my mind. Fear of this place set me right again. It serves its purpose.
MARTHA: Mad in what way?
DOCTOR: You lost your son.
SHAKESPEARE: My only boy. The Black Death took him. I wasn't even there.
MARTHA: I didn't know. I'm sorry.
SHAKESPEARE: It made me question everything. The futility of this fleeting existence. To be or not to be. Oh, that's quite good.
(Hamlet hadn't been written yet.)
DOCTOR: You should write that down.
SHAKESPEARE: Maybe not. A bit pretentious?

[Streete's cell]

(The Doctor puts his fingers on Streete's temples. It is mind meld time.)
DOCTOR: Peter, I'm the Doctor. Go into the past. One year ago. Let your mind go back. Back to when everything was fine and shining. Everything that happened in this year since happened to somebody else. It was just a story. A Winter's Tale. Let go. That's it. That's it, just let go.
(He lies Streete down on his cot.)
DOCTOR: Tell me the story, Peter. Tell me about the witches.

DOCTOR: I'm looking at the man with the words.
SHAKESPEARE: Me? But I've done nothing.
MARTHA: Hold on, though. What were you doing last night, when that Carrionite was in the room?
SHAKESPEARE: Finishing the play.
DOCTOR: What happens on the last page?
SHAKESPEARE: The boys get the girls. They have a bit of a dance. It's all as funny and thought provoking as usual. Except those last few lines. Funny thing is, I don't actually remember writing them.
DOCTOR: That's it. They used you. They gave you the final words like a spell, like a code. Love's Labours Won. It's a weapon. The right combination of words, spoken at the right place, with the shape of the Globe as an energy converter! The play's the thing! (Hamlet) And yes, you can have that.

…

DOCTOR: Good luck, Shakespeare. Once more unto the breach.
(Henry V)
SHAKESPEARE: I like that. Wait a minute, that's one of mine.
DOCTOR: (pokes his head around door) Oh, just shift!

MARTHA: The thing is, though am I missing something here? The world didn't end in 1599. It just didn't. Look at me. I'm living proof.
DOCTOR: Oh, how to explain the mechanics of the infinite temporal flux? I know. Back to the Future. It's like Back to the Future.
MARTHA: The film?
DOCTOR: No, the novelisation. Yes, the film. Marty McFly goes back and changes history.
MARTHA: And he starts fading away. Oh my God, am I going to fade?
DOCTOR: You and the entire future of the human race. It ends right now in 1599 if we don't stop it. But which house?
(A door creaks open invitingly.)
DOCTOR: Ah. Make that witch house.

(The Doctor runs out onto the stage, followed by Martha and Shakespeare.)

LILITH: The Doctor. He lives. Then watch this world become a blasted heath! (Macbeth) They come. They come!
(Lilith holds the crystal out into the red light and bat-like creatures fly into the theatre. They circle a bit then fly up into the sky.)
DOCTOR: Come on, Will! History needs you!
SHAKESPEARE: But what can I do?
DOCTOR: Reverse it!
SHAKESPEARE: How am I supposed to do that?
DOCTOR: The shape of the Globe gives words power, but you're the wordsmith, the one true genius. The only man clever enough to do it.
SHAKESPEARE: But what words? I have none ready!
DOCTOR: You're William Shakespeare!
SHAKESPEARE: But these Carrionite phrases, the need such precision.
DOCTOR: Trust yourself. When you're locked away in your room, the words just come, don't they, like magic. Words of the right sound, the right shape, the right rhythm. Words that last forever. That's what you do, Will. You choose perfect words. Do it. Improvise.
SHAKESPEARE: Close up this din of hateful, dire decay, decomposition of your witches' plot. You thieve my brains, consider me your toy. My doting Doctor tells me I am not!
LILITH: No! Words of power!
SHAKESPEARE: Foul Carrionite spectres, cease your show! Between the points
DOCTOR: Seven six one three nine oh!
SHAKESPEARE: Seven six one three nine oh! Banished like a tinker's cuss, I say to thee
MARTHA: Expelliarmus!
DOCTOR: Expelliarmus!
SHAKESPEARE: Expelliarmus!
DOCTOR: Good old JK!

(The Carrionites scream.)
LILITH: The deep darkness! They are consumed!
(The Carrionites are sucked into a tornado, along with all the extant pages of the play.)
DOCTOR: Love's Labours Won. There it goes.
(The sky clears with a flash and bang. After a few moments, someone starts clapping, then all the audience joins in.)
MARTHA: They think it was all special effects?
SHAKESPEARE: Your effect is special indeed.
MARTHA: It's not your best line.

…

(The Doctor enters wearing a small stiff ruff and carrying an animal skull.)
DOCTOR: Good props store back there. I'm not sure about this though. Reminds me of a Sycorax.
SHAKESPEARE: Sycorax. Nice word. I'll have that off you as well.
DOCTOR: I should be on ten percent. How's your head?

SHAKESPEARE: Still aching.
DOCTOR: Here, I got you this.
(The Doctor takes off the ruff and puts it on Shakespeare.)
DOCTOR: Neck brace. Wear that for a few days till it's better, although you might want to keep it. It suits you.
MARTHA: What about the play?
DOCTOR: Gone. I looked all over. Every single copy of Love's Labours Won went up in the sky.
SHAKESPEARE: My lost masterpiece.
MARTHA: You could write it up again.
DOCTOR: Yeah, better not, Will. There's still power in those words. Maybe it should best stay forgotten.
SHAKESPEARE: Oh, but I've got new ideas. Perhaps it's time I wrote about fathers and sons, in memory of my boy, my precious Hamnet.
MARTHA: Hamnet?
SHAKESPEARE: That's him.
MARTHA: Hamnet?
SHAKESPEARE: What's wrong with that?

DOCTOR: Anyway, time we were off. I've got a nice attic in the Tardis where this lot can scream for all eternity, and I've got to take Martha back to Freedonia.
SHAKESPEARE: You mean travel on through time and space.
DOCTOR: You what?
SHAKESPEARE: You're from another world like the Carrionites, and Martha is from the future. It's not hard to work out.
DOCTOR: That's incredible. You are incredible.
SHAKESPEARE: We're alike in many ways, Doctor. Martha, let me say goodbye to you in a new verse. A sonnet for my Dark Lady. Shall I compare thee to a summer's day? Thou art more lovely and more temperate.
(Burbage and Kempe enter from the street.)
BURBAGE: Will!
KEMPE: Will, you'll never believe it. She's here! She's turned up!
BURBAGE: We're the talk of the town. She heard about last night. She wants us to perform it again.
MARTHA: Who?
BURBAGE: Her Majesty. She's here.
(Fanfare and the elderly Elizabeth enters with two pikemen.)
DOCTOR: Queen Elizabeth the First!
ELIZABETH: Doctor?
DOCTOR: What?
ELIZABETH: My sworn enemy.
DOCTOR: What?
ELIZABETH: Off with his head!
DOCTOR: What?
MARTHA: Never mind what, just run! See you, Will, and thanks.
ELIZABETH: Stop that pernicious Doctor.

S3, E6 The Lazarus Experiment: Lazarus, T.S. Eliot’s poem “The Hollow Men”

The title and the name of the professor and lab refer to the Biblical story of Lazarus being raised from the dead.

LAZARUS: I find that nothing's ever exactly like you expect. There's always something to surprise you. Between the idea and the reality, between the motion and the act
DOCTOR: Falls the Shadow.
(The Hollow Men, by TS Eliot.)
LAZARUS: So the mysterious Doctor knows his Eliot. I'm impressed.

From The Hollow Men:

                       V

    Here we go round the prickly pear
    Prickly pear prickly pear

    For Thine is

8. prickly pear: cactus

S3, E7 42: The answer to the question of life, the universe, and everything

SCANNELL: Nothing's any use. We've got no engines, no time, and no chance.
DOCTOR: Oh, listen to you. Defeated before you've even started. Where's your Dunkirk spirit?

BOY: Excuse me, ma'am.
(A neat woman in starched nurses uniform meets the Doctor, who is carrying a large pile of books.)

JOAN: Oh, good morning, Mister Smith.
(He drops some of the books.)
DOCTOR: There we go.

DOCTOR: No, no, I've got it, no. Er, how best to retrieve? Tell you what. If you could take these
(Joan takes the books from his arms, and he picks up the fallen ones.)

By Christina Rossetti

Morning and evening

Maids heard the goblins cry:

“Come buy our orchard fruits,

Come buy, come buy:

Apples and quinces,

Lemons and oranges,

Plump unpeck’d cherries,

Melons and raspberries,

Bloom-down-cheek’d peaches,

Swart-headed mulberries,

Wild free-born cranberries,

Crab-apples, dewberries,

Pine-apples, blackberries,

Apricots, strawberries;—

All ripe together

In summer weather,—

Morns that pass by,

Fair eves that fly;

Come buy, come buy:

Our grapes fresh from the vine,

Pomegranates full and fine,

Dates and sharp bullaces,

Rare pears and greengages,

Damsons and bilberries,

Taste them and try:

Currants and gooseberries,

Bright-fire-like barberries,

Figs to fill your mouth,

Citrons from the South,

Sweet to tongue and sound to eye;

Come buy, come buy.”

Evening by evening

Among the brookside rushes,

Laura bow’d her head to hear,

Lizzie veil’d her blushes:

Crouching close together

In the cooling weather,

With clasping arms and cautioning lips,

With tingling cheeks and finger tips.

“Lie close,” Laura said,

Pricking up her golden head:

“We must not look at goblin men,

We must not buy their fruits:

Who knows upon what soil they fed

Their hungry thirsty roots?”

“Come buy,” call the goblins

Hobbling down the glen.

“Oh,” cried Lizzie, “Laura, Laura,

You should not peep at goblin men.”

Lizzie cover’d up her eyes,

Cover’d close lest they should look;

Laura rear’d her glossy head,

And whisper’d like the restless brook:

“Look, Lizzie, look, Lizzie,

Down the glen tramp little men.

One hauls a basket,

One bears a plate,

One lugs a golden dish

Of many pounds weight.

How fair the vine must grow

Whose grapes are so luscious;

How warm the wind must blow

Through those fruit bushes.”

“No,” said Lizzie, “No, no, no;

Their offers should not charm us,

Their evil gifts would harm us.”

She thrust a dimpled finger

Come with me home.

The stars rise, the moon bends her arc,

Each glowworm winks her spark,

Let us get home before the night grows dark:

For clouds may gather

Though this is summer weather,

Put out the lights and drench us through;

Then if we lost our way what should we do?”

Laura turn’d cold as stone

To find her sister heard that cry alone,

That goblin cry,

“Come buy our fruits, come buy.”

Must she then buy no more such dainty fruit?

Must she no more such succous pasture find,

Gone deaf and blind?

Her tree of life droop’d from the root:

She said not one word in her heart’s sore ache;

But peering thro’ the dimness, nought discerning,

Trudg’d home, her pitcher dripping all the way;

So crept to bed, and lay

Silent till Lizzie slept;

Then sat up in a passionate yearning,

And gnash’d her teeth for baulk’d desire, and wept

As if her heart would break.

Day after day, night after night,

Laura kept watch in vain

In sullen silence of exceeding pain.

She never caught again the goblin cry:

“Come buy, come buy;”—

She never spied the goblin men

Hawking their fruits along the glen:

But when the noon wax’d bright

Her hair grew thin and grey;

She dwindled, as the fair full moon doth turn

To swift decay and burn

Her fire away.

One day remembering her kernel-stone

She set it by a wall that faced the south;

Dew’d it with tears, hoped for a root,

Watch’d for a waxing shoot,

But there came none;

It never saw the sun,

It never felt the trickling moisture run:

While with sunk eyes and faded mouth

She dream’d of melons, as a traveller sees

False waves in desert drouth

With shade of leaf-crown’d trees,

And burns the thirstier in the sandful breeze.

She no more swept the house,

Tended the fowls or cows,

Fetch’d honey, kneaded cakes of wheat,

Brought water from the brook:

But sat down listless in the chimney-nook

And would not eat.

Tender Lizzie could not bear

To watch her sister’s cankerous care

Yet not to share.

She night and morning

Caught the goblins’ cry:

“Come buy our orchard fruits,

Come buy, come buy;”—

Beside the brook, along the glen,

She heard the tramp of goblin men,

The yoke and stir

Poor Laura could not hear;

Long’d to buy fruit to comfort her,

But fear’d to pay too dear.

She thought of Jeanie in her grave,

Who should have been a bride;

But who for joys brides hope to have

Fell sick and died

In her gay prime,

In earliest winter time

With the first glazing rime,

With the first snow-fall of crisp winter time.

Till Laura dwindling

Seem’d knocking at Death’s door:

Then Lizzie weigh’d no more

Better and worse;

But put a silver penny in her purse,

Kiss’d Laura, cross’d the heath with clumps of furze

At twilight, halted by the brook:

And for the first time in her life

Began to listen and look.

Laugh’d every goblin

When they spied her peeping:

Came towards her hobbling,

Flying, running, leaping,

Puffing and blowing,

Chuckling, clapping, crowing,

Clucking and gobbling,

Mopping and mowing,

Full of airs and graces,

Pulling wry faces,

Demure grimaces,

Cat-like and rat-like,

Ratel- and wombat-like,

Snail-paced in a hurry,

Parrot-voiced and whistler,

Helter skelter, hurry skurry,

Chattering like magpies,

Fluttering like pigeons,

Gliding like fishes,—

Hugg’d her and kiss’d her:

Squeez’d and caress’d her:

Stretch’d up their dishes,

Panniers, and plates:

“Look at our apples

Russet and dun,

Bob at our cherries,

Bite at our peaches,

Citrons and dates,

Grapes for the asking,

Pears red with basking

Out in the sun,

Plums on their twigs;

Pluck them and suck them,

Pomegranates, figs.”—

“Good folk,” said Lizzie,

Mindful of Jeanie:

“Give me much and many: —

Held out her apron,

Toss’d them her penny.

“Nay, take a seat with us,

Honour and eat with us,”

They answer’d grinning:

“Our feast is but beginning.

Night yet is early,

Warm and dew-pearly,

Wakeful and starry:

Such fruits as these

No man can carry:

Half their bloom would fly,

Half their dew would dry,

Half their flavour would pass by.

Sit down and feast with us,

Be welcome guest with us,

Cheer you and rest with us.”—

“Thank you,” said Lizzie: “But one waits

At home alone for me:

So without further parleying,

If you will not sell me any

Of your fruits though much and many,

Give me back my silver penny

I toss’d you for a fee.”—

They began to scratch their pates,

No longer wagging, purring,

But visibly demurring,

Grunting and snarling.

One call’d her proud,

Cross-grain’d, uncivil;

Their tones wax’d loud,

Their looks were evil.

Lashing their tails

They trod and hustled her,

Elbow’d and jostled her,

Claw’d with their nails,

Barking, mewing, hissing, mocking,

Tore her gown and soil’d her stocking,

Twitch’d her hair out by the roots,

Stamp’d upon her tender feet,

Held her hands and squeez’d their fruits

Against her mouth to make her eat.

White and golden Lizzie stood,

Like a lily in a flood,—

Like a rock of blue-vein’d stone

Lash’d by tides obstreperously,—

Like a beacon left alone

In a hoary roaring sea,

Sending up a golden fire,—

Like a fruit-crown’d orange-tree

White with blossoms honey-sweet

Sore beset by wasp and bee,—

Like a royal virgin town

Topp’d with gilded dome and spire

Close beleaguer’d by a fleet

Mad to tug her standard down.

One may lead a horse to water,

Twenty cannot make him drink.

Though the goblins cuff’d and caught her,

Coax’d and fought her,

Bullied and besought her,

Scratch’d her, pinch’d her black as ink,

Kick’d and knock’d her,

Maul’d and mock’d her,

Lizzie utter’d not a word;

Would not open lip from lip

Lest they should cram a mouthful in:

But laugh’d in heart to feel the drip

Of juice that syrupp’d all her face,

And lodg’d in dimples of her chin,

And streak’d her neck which quaked like curd.

At last the evil people,

Worn out by her resistance,

Flung back her penny, kick’d their fruit

Along whichever road they took,

Not leaving root or stone or shoot;

Some writh’d into the ground,

Some div’d into the brook

With ring and ripple,

Some scudded on the gale without a sound,

Some vanish’d in the distance.

In a smart, ache, tingle,

Lizzie went her way;

Knew not was it night or day;

Sprang up the bank, tore thro’ the furze,

Threaded copse and dingle,

And heard her penny jingle

Bouncing in her purse,—

Its bounce was music to her ear.

She ran and ran

As if she fear’d some goblin man

Dogg’d her with gibe or curse

Or something worse:

But not one goblin scurried after,

Nor was she prick’d by fear;

The kind heart made her windy-paced

That urged her home quite out of breath with haste

And inward laughter.

She cried, “Laura,” up the garden,

“Did you miss me?

Come and kiss me.

Never mind my bruises,

Hug me, kiss me, suck my juices

Squeez’d from goblin fruits for you,

Goblin pulp and goblin dew.

Eat me, drink me, love me;

Laura, make much of me;

For your sake I have braved the glen

And had to do with goblin merchant men.”

Laura started from her chair,

Flung her arms up in the air,

Clutch’d her hair:

“Lizzie, Lizzie, have you tasted

For my sake the fruit forbidden?

Must your light like mine be hidden,

Your young life like mine be wasted,

Undone in mine undoing,

And ruin’d in my ruin,

Thirsty, canker’d, goblin-ridden?”—

She clung about her sister,

Kiss’d and kiss’d and kiss’d her:

Tears once again

Refresh’d her shrunken eyes,

Dropping like rain

After long sultry drouth;

Shaking with aguish fear, and pain,

She kiss’d and kiss’d her with a hungry mouth.

Her lips began to scorch,

That juice was wormwood to her tongue,

She loath’d the feast:

Writhing as one possess’d she leap’d and sung,

Rent all her robe, and wrung

Her hands in lamentable haste,

And beat her breast.

Her locks stream’d like the torch

Borne by a racer at full speed,

Or like the mane of horses in their flight,

Or like an eagle when she stems the light

Straight toward the sun,

Or like a caged thing freed,

Or like a flying flag when armies run.

Swift fire spread through her veins, knock’d at her heart,

Met the fire smouldering there

And overbore its lesser flame;

She gorged on bitterness without a name:

Ah! fool, to choose such part

Of soul-consuming care!

Sense fail’d in the mortal strife:

Like the watch-tower of a town

Which an earthquake shatters down,

Like a lightning-stricken mast,

Like a wind-uprooted tree

Spun about,

Like a foam-topp’d waterspout

Cast down headlong in the sea,

She fell at last;

Pleasure past and anguish past,

Is it death or is it life?

Life out of death.

That night long Lizzie watch’d by her,

Counted her pulse’s flagging stir,

Felt for her breath,

Held water to her lips, and cool’d her face

With tears and fanning leaves:

But when the first birds chirp’d about their eaves,

And early reapers plodded to the place

Of golden sheaves,

And dew-wet grass

Bow’d in the morning winds so brisk to pass,

And new buds with new day

Open’d of cup-like lilies on the stream,

Laura awoke as from a dream,

Laugh’d in the innocent old way,

Hugg’d Lizzie but not twice or thrice;

Her gleaming locks show’d not one thread of grey,

Her breath was sweet as May

And light danced in her eyes.

Days, weeks, months, years

Afterwards, when both were wives

With children of their own;

Their mother-hearts beset with fears,

Their lives bound up in tender lives;

Laura would call the little ones

And tell them of her early prime,

Those pleasant days long gone

Of not-returning time:

Would talk about the haunted glen,

The wicked, quaint fruit-merchant men,

Their fruits like honey to the throat

But poison in the blood;

(Men sell not such in any town):

Would tell them how her sister stood

In deadly peril to do her good,

And win the fiery antidote:

Then joining hands to little hands

Would bid them cling together,

“For there is no friend like a sister

In calm or stormy weather;

To cheer one on the tedious way,

To fetch one if one goes astray,

To lift one if one totters down,

To strengthen whilst one stands.”

Every good gothic manor needs a ghost. This one's from Crimson Peak. I don't watch a lot of movies, but this one is one of my favourites. I do, however, read a lot of gothic fiction.

Notes about Gothic Literature

✓American Gothic Fiction Alan Lloyd-Smith (library textbook):

“the message of Gothic…is that it isn’t so much a matter of whether you can repeat the past as whether the past will repeat itself in you” (p.1)

“But in this enigmatic American erosion the Gothic object is allowed its own life, remaining stubbornly resistant to interpretation, however persuasive” (p.74)

“A all these instances suggest, domestic Gothic is intimately bound up with the idea of the house, gender, and the family, which becomes, through metaphor, a way of externalizing the inner life of fictional characters” (p.102)

‘“The past isn’t dead,” says one of Faulkner’s characters, “it isn’t even past,” which might serve as a motto for American Gothic itself as it explores the tensions between a culturally sanctioned progressive optimism and an actual dark legacy.’ (p.118)

✓Unsettled Remains: Canadian Literature and the Postcolonial Gothic, Edited by Cynthia Sugars and Gerry Turcotte 

“Initially, it is fair to say, the Gothic emerged as a way of responding to the unfamiliar by demonizing and even fetishizing the “unknown” – be it human or landscape. Often this monstrous presence was figured as an Indigenous one – a danger lying just beyond the garrison but not sufficiently removed. Over time, Canadian writers began to appropriate this force, to bend it to a national purpose, and to map the parameters of an identity that might embrace what was resonantly local so that the Gothic became a way to insist on, rather than deny, a colonial history. In effect, the gothic mode was used to articulate a suitably “haunted” version of the Canadian identity, one that lent the Canadian locale a “feel” of authenticity because it had been rendered “(un)homely” (that is, both familiar and unfamiliar at the same time).” (p.xvii)

‘“The white Canadian looks at the Indian. The Indian is Other and therefore alien. But the Indian is indigenous and therefore cannot be alien. So the Canadian must be alien. But how can the Canadian be alien within Canada? –Terry Coldie, Fear and Temptation’ (Brian Johnson, p.25).

“Since 2001,,...much important work has been done on the Gothic in English-Canadian literature, including Justin Edwards’s Gothic Canada: Reading the Spectre of a National Literature (2005) and a 2006 special issue of University of Toronto Quarterly, guest edited by Marlene Goldman and Joanne Saul. Most relevant to this essay is Jodey Castricano’s ‘Learning to Talk with Ghosts: Canadian Gothic and the Poetics of Haunting in Eden Robinson’s Monkey Beach,’” (Jennifer Andrews, p.206).

✓Gothic Literature by Sue Chaplin

“Recent work in Gothic criticism has argued that the Gothic ought not to be defined in terms of its emotional or aesthetic effect, or even regarded as a literary ‘genre’ at all (that is to say, as a class of texts conforming to particular conventions of content and/or style). Rather, it should be considered a ‘mode’ of writing that responds in certain diverse yet recognisable ways to the conflicts and anxieties of its historical moment and that is characterised especially by its capacity to represent individual and societal traumas” (p.4)

“These Gothic interventions into other genres of literature are discussed in Part Three…and it will be seen that during this period the mutable quality of the Gothic became, paradoxically, one of its characteristics features; ‘paradoxically’ because the very quality of mutability is what makes it so difficult to ‘characterise’ the Gothic, to identify its defining qualities as a literary category.” (p.20)

Painting: The Passage of St Gothard by Salvator Rosa

Byron’s poems Giaour and Manfred

Angela Carter’s The Bloody Chamber

Jamaica Kincaid’s The Autobiography of My Mother

“Gothic tends to foreground what other forms of writing (the realist novel, for example) often seek to conceal: that its narratives are not necessarily trustworthy; that literary conventions bear a slippery relationship to the ‘truths’ they mean to communicate.” (p.182)

“In [Jane Eyre and ‘The Yellow Wallpaper’], women are portrayed as susceptible to madness, but their mental trauma is not depicted as somehow innate to their femininity; rather, it is related to and emanates from social situations that render the female protagonist vulnerable, alienated and desperate.” (p.213)

item.title: ✨ The Super Power of being a Multi-Passionate Creative ✨
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded: In this video, I loved her metaphor about being multi passionate as being soil that needs companion planting or rotation so as not to be depleted or to be able to be refilled when you are depleted. She also talked about not wanting to master anything but preferring to be in a relationship with her gifts. I do enjoying think of my art as a conversation I’m having with the materials and subject matter. And I have no interest in limiting myself to a single medium or interest. I need space to wander.

item.title: I don't want a job. I want to make art.
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded:
I stumbled upon Alecia Renece The Artist on YouTube this week and I love her already. I see some binge watching in my future. She’s so poetic.
I’m not at a point in my life where I want to turn my art into a job, certainly not a full-time job, because I feel like that would ruin the freedom it currently gives me, but I agree with her all the same. Capitalism has made it so hard for everyone to be fully-expressed human beings who can create and feel deeply.

item.title: Granulating Gouache
item.dc:creator: nicolejaynebergen
item.content:encoded: The permanent (hansa) yellow and burnt umber didn’t granulate much. The ultramarine and iris (has dioxazine purple and fluorescents but also ultramarine) did the best. The pure red (naphthol), opera (fluorescent pink), and magenta were middling. For these ones, it seemed to be a balance of getting enough but not too much pigment in a lot of water. The gold seems to have granulated a bit too – I guess that’s the mica. This is in a royal talens sketchbook.
